questions.title: Writer and reader synchronize on different locks
questions.task: Explain why both methods being synchronized blocks does not publish data and ready correctly. Use one happens-before path.
questions.expectedBehavior: If reader observes ready, it must observe data=42.
questions.answer: Unlocking writeLock has no happens-before relation to later locking readLock. The accesses still race.
questions.explanation: Monitor visibility requires the same monitor. Use one lock for both, or publish with a volatile ready flag written after data and read before data. Different locks provide independent ordering domains.
hints: Which monitor edge does JLS define?
keyTakeaways: Same-monitor unlock/lock creates happens-before.
Different locks do not coordinate.
Both readers and writers follow one protocol.
followUpQuestions: How would volatile ready publish data?
Would volatile data alone protect the pair?

questions.title: Volatile flag is written before the data
questions.task: The reader can observe ready=true and stale data. Reverse the publication order and prove the happens-before chain.
questions.expectedBehavior: A reader that sees ready=true sees data=42.
questions.answer: The volatile write occurs before data=42, so it cannot publish a later ordinary write to a reader after the volatile read.
questions.explanation: Program order must be data=42 then volatile ready=true. The volatile write happens-before a subsequent read that observes it; transitivity carries the preceding data write to the reader's later data read.
hints: Which ordinary writes occur before the volatile write?
questions.correctedCode: void write(){ data=42; ready=true; }
keyTakeaways: Publication order matters.
Volatile write publishes preceding actions.
Reader checks volatile before dependent fields.

How would an immutable snapshot simplify this?

questions.title: Thread.start safely publishes pre-start configuration
questions.task: Determine whether volatile is required for input written before start and output read after join. State both lifecycle happens-before rules.
questions.expectedBehavior: Print 42 with no data race under the shown ordering.
questions.answer: The code correctly prints 42. Pre-start actions happen-before worker actions, and worker actions happen-before successful join return.
questions.explanation: input does not need volatile because start publishes earlier configuration. output does not need volatile because join publishes worker completion. Mutating input after start or reading output before join would require separate coordination.

keyTakeaways: start publishes prior actions to the child.
join publishes child actions to the joiner.
Use lifecycle edges instead of redundant volatile fields.

What if join times out?

questions.title: this escapes from constructor
questions.task: The constructor starts a thread before all fields are assigned. Explain how the callback can observe partial state and refactor construction/publication.
questions.expectedBehavior: No other thread obtains this until construction finishes.
questions.answer: The code also fails definite assignment for final id usage before assignment; more generally, starting a thread from a constructor exposes this before construction and can observe partial/default state.
questions.explanation: Complete all final/nonfinal initialization, return the object, then let an owner start/register it. Final-field guarantees assume proper construction without escape. Avoid overridable callbacks/listener registration/thread start inside constructors.
hints: When does the new thread receive this?
Has the constructor completed?

Complete immutable state before start/registration.
Final fields have special safe-construction semantics.

How do factories help?

questions.title: final List reference is still mutable shared state
questions.task: Explain why final does not make concurrent add/iteration safe and publish an immutable value instead.
questions.expectedBehavior: Readers see a stable immutable list without concurrent mutation.
questions.answer: final prevents reassigning names but does not synchronize or freeze ArrayList contents. Concurrent add/iteration is a data race and can fail.
questions.explanation: Use a lock for mutation/traversal, a concurrent structure with fitting semantics, or replace immutable snapshots through volatile/AtomicReference. Ownership and mutability are distinct from reference reassignment.
hints: What operation does final prohibit?
keyTakeaways: final reference is not deep immutability.
ArrayList remains non-thread-safe.
Immutable snapshot replacement enables lock-free reads.
followUpQuestions: Why is names volatile in the snapshot version?
When would CopyOnWriteArrayList fit?

questions.title: Thread.onSpinWait does not create visibility
questions.task: The loop calls onSpinWait and assumes it refreshes done. Explain the data race and add a proper synchronization mechanism.
questions.expectedBehavior: Worker termination is observed portably.
questions.answer: onSpinWait is a processor/runtime hint for spin loops, not a memory synchronization action. done remains a racy ordinary field and the loop may not terminate.
questions.explanation: Use volatile/AtomicBoolean for a spin flag, or better join/latch when waiting for completion. Spinning consumes CPU and should be reserved for measured low-latency designs.
hints: Does onSpinWait appear in JMM synchronizes-with rules?
keyTakeaways: CPU hints do not create happens-before.
Use join for completion.
Avoid wasteful spins without measured need.

multithreading.title: Locks, Conditions & Atomics
multithreading.summary: Debug explicit-lock cleanup, Condition ownership/guard loops, read/write effects, CAS retries, side-effectful update functions, ABA/versioning, and LongAdder limitations.
learningGoals: Unlock exactly once in finally.
Await conditions under their associated lock and while predicate.
Keep CAS functions side-effect-free.
Use a lock/immutable aggregate for multi-field invariants.

questions.title: Exception leaks ReentrantLock
questions.task: Explain why later callers block forever when update throws and apply the canonical pattern.
questions.expectedBehavior: Release the lock on normal and abrupt completion.
questions.answer: risky throws before unlock, leaving the lock owned. Subsequent threads block.
questions.explanation: Place unlock in finally immediately after successful lock acquisition. ReentrantLock does not have structured automatic release like synchronized.
hints: Which statement is skipped after throw?
keyTakeaways: Explicit locks require explicit finally cleanup.
Acquire then immediately enter try.
Exceptions must not leak ownership.
followUpQuestions: How does tryLock change the pattern?
Why might synchronized be safer here?

questions.title: Condition await called without lock
questions.task: Predict the failure and implement the guarded-wait pattern.
questions.expectedBehavior: Wait while empty, then remove after signal under the same lock.
questions.answer: await throws IllegalMonitorStateException because the current thread does not hold the associated lock.
questions.explanation: Acquire lock, test predicate in while, await (which releases/reacquires the lock), update state, and unlock in finally. Signallers also hold the lock and change state before signal.
hints: What ownership does Condition require?
Why while rather than if?
keyTakeaways: Condition is bound to one Lock.
await in a while predicate loop.
unlock in finally.
followUpQuestions: When use signalAll?
How does await compare with Object.wait?

questions.title: Atomic update function sends duplicate emails
questions.task: updateAndGet may invoke its function more than once under CAS contention. Explain why the side effect can repeat and separate atomic state calculation from effects.
questions.expectedBehavior: State transition is atomic and email is emitted once only after this call wins the transition.
questions.answer: CAS update functions may be retried if another thread changes state. sendEmail can run multiple times even though one value is installed.
questions.explanation: Keep update functions pure. For a one-way transition, compareAndSet NEW->RUNNING and send only when it returns true. Even then, a crash between state and email may require an outbox/idempotency design for exactly-once business effects.
hints: Can updateAndGet retry its function?
Which boolean operation reports the winning transition?
keyTakeaways: CAS functions may retry.
Keep atomic update functions side-effect-free.
External exactly-once effects need stronger protocols.
followUpQuestions: What is ABA?
How would an outbox help?

questions.title: Two AtomicIntegers do not preserve one invariant
questions.task: A transfer decrements available then increments reserved. Readers can observe an invalid total. Preserve the pair as one atomic state transition.
questions.expectedBehavior: available + reserved always equals capacity for every observed version.
questions.answer: Each variable update is atomic, but the pair is not. A reader can run between operations and observe total 9.
questions.explanation: Use one lock guarding both fields or one AtomicReference to an immutable record and update the whole pair with one CAS. Independent atomics do not create a multi-variable transaction.
hints: How many linearization points exist?
keyTakeaways: Atomic variables protect individual values.
Cross-field invariants need one atomic boundary.
Immutable aggregate CAS is one option.
followUpQuestions: When is a lock simpler?
Can the update function have side effects?

questions.title: LongAdder sum is used as a hard limit
questions.task: Multiple threads use LongAdder.sum before increment to enforce max 10 active jobs. Explain why more than 10 can start and choose an exact primitive.
questions.expectedBehavior: Check-and-increment the hard limit atomically.
questions.answer: sum and increment are separate, and LongAdder sum is not an atomic snapshot under concurrent updates. Many threads can pass before increments become visible in the sum.
questions.explanation: LongAdder is for scalable statistics, not hard limits. Use a Semaphore(10), or an AtomicInteger CAS loop/lock that combines check and increment. Semaphore directly models permits and supports release/fairness/timed acquisition.
hints: Is sum+increment one operation?
Which concurrent primitive models 10 permits?
keyTakeaways: LongAdder favors throughput statistics.
Its sum is not a hard-limit transaction.
Semaphore models bounded concurrent permits.
followUpQuestions: What if exit releases twice?
When use AtomicInteger instead?

questions.title: Read lock attempts unsafe upgrade
questions.task: A method holds ReentrantReadWriteLock.readLock and calls writeLock.lock when cache is missing. Explain the deadlock/upgrade hazard and use release-then-acquire with recheck.
questions.expectedBehavior: No thread waits for a write lock while retaining a read hold that prevents that write lock.
questions.answer: ReentrantReadWriteLock does not safely support upgrading a held read lock to write. The thread can wait for all readers—including its own read hold—to release.
questions.explanation: Release the read lock, acquire write, recheck because another writer may have initialized, update, then optionally downgrade by acquiring read before releasing write. Simpler synchronized/volatile initialization may be preferable.
hints: Can write lock be granted while any read hold remains?
Why recheck after acquiring write?
keyTakeaways: Read-to-write upgrade is hazardous.
Release, acquire write, and recheck.
Use simpler synchronization unless read/write benefits are measured.
followUpQuestions: How does lock downgrading work?
Would volatile double-check be simpler?

multithreading.title: Executors, Futures & CompletableFuture
multithreading.summary: Debug pool admission, unbounded queues, starvation, ignored Future failures, timeout/cancel semantics, CompletableFuture executor selection/composition, periodic-task failure, and two-phase shutdown.
learningGoals: Treat pool/queue/rejection as overload policy.
Observe asynchronous failures and cancellations.
Avoid blocking dependency cycles.
Own and shut down executors correctly.

questions.title: Unbounded queue makes maximumPoolSize ineffective
questions.task: A ThreadPoolExecutor has core=2, max=20, but only two workers process a huge backlog. Explain admission behavior and configure bounded overload policy.
questions.expectedBehavior: Queue capacity and rejection reflect downstream throughput instead of unbounded latency/memory.
questions.answer: The unbounded queue accepts tasks after core threads are busy, so the executor normally never creates workers beyond core and max=20 has no practical effect.
questions.explanation: ThreadPoolExecutor admission is core workers -> queue -> extra up to max if queue is full -> rejection. Use a deliberate bounded queue and rejection policy after measuring CPU/I/O/downstream capacity. More threads are not free and can overload dependencies.
hints: When are threads beyond core created?
Can this queue become full in practice?
keyTakeaways: Unbounded queue hides overload.
max threads activate only after queue rejection/fullness.
Capacity/rejection are reliability decisions.
followUpQuestions: How does CallerRuns create backpressure?
How would CPU-bound sizing differ?

questions.title: Fixed pool starves on child Future.get
questions.task: Two parent tasks occupy both workers, submit child tasks to the same pool, and block on get. Explain task-dependency starvation and refactor with non-blocking composition or separate ownership.
questions.expectedBehavior: Child work can execute without requiring a worker held by its waiting parent.
questions.answer: Both workers run parents and wait for children queued to the same pool. No worker remains to run children, so progress stops.
questions.explanation: This is thread-pool starvation/dependency deadlock, not a monitor cycle. Avoid blocking inside tasks for same-pool children. Compose CompletableFutures, compute child inline, use a work-stealing design appropriate to tasks, or separate executors with bounded capacity based on dependency domains.
hints: How many workers are free after parents start?
Where are child tasks?
keyTakeaways: Blocking child dependencies can starve a fixed pool.
Use non-blocking stage composition.
Diagnose task dependency, not only lock cycles.
followUpQuestions: Can CompletableFuture still starve if a stage calls join?
When use separate executors?

questions.title: Future timeout leaves work running
questions.task: Caller times out and assumes the task stopped. Explain the lifecycle and explicitly decide cancellation.
questions.expectedBehavior: After timeout, request interruption when appropriate and handle non-cooperative work honestly.
questions.answer: Timed get only stops the caller from waiting; the task may continue using resources and later complete.
questions.explanation: Call cancel(true) if interruption is an appropriate cooperative cancellation request, and design slowCall to honor it/API-specific timeouts. cancel does not roll back completed side effects or forcibly stop non-interruptible operations.
hints: What method changes Future cancellation state?
keyTakeaways: Timeout and cancellation differ.
cancel(true) is a request.
Underlying APIs need their own deadlines/cancellation.
followUpQuestions: What does get throw after successful cancellation?
Can CompletableFuture orTimeout interrupt its supplier?

questions.title: thenApply creates nested CompletableFuture
questions.task: A function already returns CompletableFuture<Order>. Explain why thenApply produces CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Order>> and flatten it.
questions.expectedBehavior: One CompletableFuture<Order> that completes when the async order lookup completes.
questions.answer: thenApply maps T to U exactly; here U itself is CompletableFuture<Order>. Use thenCompose to flatten dependent asynchronous stages.
questions.explanation: thenCompose is the async analogue of flatMap. thenCombine is for independent stages whose results are combined. Executor choice matters: Async variants without explicit executor use the common pool.

thenCompose flattens dependent async work.
thenCombine joins independent stages.

How would failures be recovered?

questions.title: Periodic task silently stops after one exception
questions.task: A scheduled heartbeat runs twice and then never again after a RuntimeException. Explain ScheduledExecutorService periodic semantics and keep expected failures observable while continuing.
questions.expectedBehavior: Each scheduled run handles expected failure and the periodic series continues according to policy.
questions.buggyCode:
ScheduledExecutorService s=Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(1);
s.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> sendHeartbeat(),0,1,SECONDS);
questions.answer: If a periodic execution throws and the exception escapes, subsequent executions are suppressed.
questions.explanation: Catch expected operational exceptions inside the Runnable, record/metric them, and decide whether continuing is safe. Do not catch fatal programming/invariant problems merely to keep a corrupt loop alive. Retain ScheduledFuture for cancellation/status and shut down the scheduler owner.
hints: What does the periodic scheduling contract say after exceptional execution?
keyTakeaways: Escaping failure stops future periodic executions.
Handle expected failures inside task.
Retain lifecycle ownership and observability.
followUpQuestions: Fixed rate versus fixed delay?
Can one execution overlap itself?

questions.title: shutdownNow is treated as guaranteed termination
questions.task: The application calls shutdownNow and immediately closes shared files while tasks may still run. Implement two-phase shutdown and explain cooperation.
questions.expectedBehavior: Stop submissions, wait, request interruption, wait again, and close shared resources only after termination/explicit failure policy.
questions.buggyCode:
pool.shutdownNow();
sharedFile.close();
questions.answer: shutdownNow only attempts to interrupt active tasks and returns queued never-started tasks. It does not wait or guarantee that tasks terminate.
questions.explanation: Use shutdown, awaitTermination, then shutdownNow if the deadline expires, then await again. Preserve caller interruption and handle queued returned tasks. Tasks must honor interruption; non-interruptible code can outlive the request.

What does shutdownNow return?
keyTakeaways: shutdownNow is best effort and non-waiting.
Use two-phase owner shutdown.
Tasks must cooperate with interruption.

multithreading.title: Interruption, Cancellation & Shutdown
multithreading.summary: Debug interrupt-status clearing, propagation/restoration, CPU-loop cancellation points, Future.cancel, timeout versus cancellation, resource/invariant cleanup, and executor ownership.
learningGoals: Treat interrupt as cooperative request.
Know isInterrupted versus Thread.interrupted.
Make blocking and CPU tasks cancellation-responsive.
Preserve invariants and lifecycle ownership.

questions.title: Thread.interrupted clears the signal in a loop condition
questions.task: The loop calls Thread.interrupted twice per iteration and misses a signal during cleanup logic. Explain clearing behavior and use a non-clearing check.
questions.expectedBehavior: Once interruption is requested, the loop exits and status remains available to outer code if policy requires.
questions.answer: Thread.interrupted checks the current thread and clears status. The first or second check can consume the signal, making later checks false.
questions.explanation: Use isInterrupted for non-clearing observation. Use Thread.interrupted only when intentionally consuming the signal. A single owner should define whether status is restored before return.
hints: Which check has a clearing side effect?
questions.correctedCode: while(!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()){ doWork(); }

isInterrupted does not clear.
Cancellation policy owns consumption/restoration.

questions.title: CPU loop ignores Future.cancel(true)
questions.task: cancel(true) returns true but a prime-search loop keeps using CPU. Add bounded cancellation checks and define partial-result behavior.
questions.expectedBehavior: Task exits promptly after interrupt without corrupting shared output.
questions.answer: The loop never blocks or checks interrupt status, so interruption request does not force it to stop.
questions.explanation: Check isInterrupted at sensible batch intervals and exit/throw CancellationException. Stage results locally and commit at safe boundaries so cancellation cannot expose half-updated state. API calls inside isPrime/save may need their own cancellation rules.

keyTakeaways: Interrupt cannot forcibly stop CPU code.
Add cooperative cancellation points.
Preserve state invariants on exit.

questions.title: InterruptedException is wrapped without restoring status
questions.task: A Runnable adapter wraps InterruptedException in a domain exception. Preserve both cancellation status and cause.
questions.expectedBehavior: Outer executor/lifecycle code can observe interruption, and diagnostics retain the original exception.
questions.buggyCode:
try{queue.take();}
catch(InterruptedException e){throw new WorkerException("failed");}
questions.answer: The thrown InterruptedException cleared status, and the wrapper discards its cause. Cancellation is misclassified as ordinary failure.
questions.explanation: Usually restore status and return from Runnable. If translation is required, restore and pass cause, while ensuring the owner treats the domain type as cancellation rather than retryable failure.
hints: What two pieces of information are lost?
keyTakeaways: Propagate or restore interruption.
Preserve causes during translation.
Normal shutdown may not be an error.

questions.title: Timeout fallback races with a continuing side effect
questions.task: Caller returns “not charged” after timeout while background payment may complete. Explain unknown outcome and design idempotent/cancellable operation semantics.
questions.expectedBehavior: Never claim failure/success without reconciling operation state; retries are deduplicated.
questions.answer: The timeout only stops waiting; charge may complete afterward. Returning notCharged can be false and a retry can double-charge.

Can the server have committed before response?

Cancellation is best effort.
Side effects need idempotency/reconciliation.

questions.title: Cancellation leaves lock-protected state half transitioned
questions.task: An interruptible call occurs between decrement and increment of one invariant. Ensure cancellation restores/commits atomically before releasing the lock.
questions.expectedBehavior: Invariant available+reserved remains constant even if interrupted.
questions.answer: If remoteAudit is interrupted, available is decremented but reserved is not incremented; finally releases the lock with a broken invariant.
questions.explanation: Do not perform slow/interruptible external calls inside a critical state transition. Stage/commit local invariant atomically, release lock, then audit via an outbox/event, or compensate under the lock before propagating interruption. finally guarantees release, not rollback.

keyTakeaways: finally releases resources but does not rollback state.
Keep blocking external calls outside locks.
Cancellation-safe design preserves invariants.

questions.title: Library shuts down an executor it borrowed
questions.task: A helper receives a shared ExecutorService, submits one task, and shuts it down. Explain why unrelated application tasks are later rejected and fix lifecycle ownership.

type-casting.title: Type Casting
type-casting.summary: Practice primitive widening and narrowing, reference upcasting and downcasting, instanceof, polymorphism, ClassCastException, and compile-time versus runtime type rules.
learningGoals: Distinguish primitive casting from reference casting.
Understand widening and narrowing conversions.

questions.title: Widening primitive conversion
questions.task: Predict the output and explain why an explicit cast is not required.

questions.answer: The output is 100.0.
questions.explanation: Assigning int to double is a widening primitive conversion. Java can perform this conversion implicitly because the destination type has a wider range/representation for this conversion.
hints: Compare the source and destination primitive types.

questions.title: Upcasting is implicit and safe
questions.task: Explain why a subclass object can be assigned to a superclass reference without an explicit cast.
questions.expectedBehavior: The assignment compiles and the overridden method uses dynamic dispatch.
questions.answer: The output is Dog.
questions.explanation: Assigning Dog to an Animal reference is upcasting and is implicit. The reference can access members defined by Animal, but overridden instance methods use the runtime object's implementation, so Dog.sound() executes.

animal.sound();
keyTakeaways: Upcasting from subclass to superclass is implicit.
Polymorphic method dispatch uses the runtime object.

questions.title: Primitive narrowing overflow
questions.task: Predict the result of narrowing a large int to byte and explain the overflow behavior.
questions.expectedBehavior: The result must be explained using the low-order bits retained by the narrowing conversion.
questions.answer: The output is -126.
questions.explanation: byte is an 8-bit signed type. Narrowing from int to byte retains the low-order 8 bits, which represent -126 in signed byte form. The conversion does not throw an exception for this numeric narrowing.

keyTakeaways: Narrowing numeric conversion can change the value.

questions.task: Correct the code so that process() invokes drive only for Car objects.

questions.title: Reference type controls accessible methods
questions.task: Explain why the compiler rejects the direct call to the subclass-specific method.
questions.expectedBehavior: The code should compile only after a valid downcast.

questions.title: Casting does not change the object
questions.task: Explain what changes when a reference is cast and what remains unchanged about the actual object.
questions.expectedBehavior: The cast changes the reference's compile-time view, not the runtime object's class.
questions.answer: The output is Bark followed by Dog. Casting does not create a new Dog or change the object's runtime type; it changes how the existing reference is viewed by the compiler.
questions.explanation: animal and dog refer to the same Dog object. The cast enables access to Dog-specific members through the dog reference. The runtime class remains Dog throughout.
hints: How many objects are created?

questions.correctedCode:
Animal animal = new Dog();
Dog dog = (Dog) animal; // same object, narrower reference type
keyTakeaways: Casting a reference does not create a new object.
The same object can be viewed through different reference types.
Runtime class remains unchanged after a reference cast.
